items.title: Why is JJ Gabriel in Man Utd's team photo?
items.content: <article>BBC Sport Manchester United reporter Simon Stone gives an update on 16-year-old JJ Gabriel's future at the club after the teenager was included in the club's official team photo.</article>

items.title: Gabriel in Man Utd team photo but no hint of reconciliation
items.content: <article>As he prepares to celebrate his 16th birthday, the rift between Manchester United and JJ Gabriel shows no sign of being healed.</article>
items.lbText:
JJ Gabriel has been included in Manchester United's official team photo for this season but there remains no hint of a reconciliation with the club as new details of his efforts to leave Old Trafford emerge.

The teenage forward - who turns 16 on Tuesday - features in the photographs that were released on Monday.

It is understood the pictures were taken on 8 September - two days before he played his final game for the club and informed them of his intention to leave.

It is virtually certain his next involvement in a United game will be as an opposition player.

United still hold his registration and, according to sources close to Old Trafford, the club have made multiple attempts to reconcile the situation as part of their duty of care to the teenager. So far, it has been to no avail.

Gabriel is now a target for several of Europe's top clubs, with Real Madrid and Barcelona among those taking a keen interest. He now has a European Union passport, which is thought could smooth his passage to the continent.

However, while no clubs have approached United so far, they would consider legal action if any evidence of an illegal inducement by a club or agent - that would contravene regulations in relation to young players - was to emerge.

While tensions between Gabriel's camp and United had been simmering for a number of months, sources have told BBC Sport the player's decision to seek a move away was ultimately triggered by his non-inclusion in Michael Carrick’s side for the Champions League encounter with Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK on 10 September.

The youngster's camp had expressed a desire for Gabriel to be used as a substitute against Sabah - which, on paper, was the easiest of United's league-phase games.

Sources say the prospect of the Londoner coming on against Brighton in the EFL Cup on 16 September was also discussed, with United officials subsequently insistent that was the plan.

Had he played in either match, Gabriel would have become United's youngest ever player.

However, by the time the encounter with Fabian Hurzeler's side arrived, the striker had already told the club of his intention to quit and had left the country.

Gabriel could not play against Sabah because he had not been registered on United's Uefa A list of players when it was announced on 3 September. The precise reasons for this have not been made clear.

It did not prevent him scoring a hat-trick in a Uefa Youth League game against them at Leigh Sports Village earlier on 10 September. While he has not been back to United since, it is not clear whether anything significant happened after that game.

For their part, United believe they made it clear they view Gabriel as immensely important to their first-team future, even though sources have indicated the player did not report for the start of the academy's pre-season training schedule at the beginning of July - a week earlier than the senior squad - despite being asked to do so.

Sources also say they lobbied the Premier League to allow the forward to use "JJ Gabriel" on the back of his shirt - which they believe underlined their commitment to the academy prospect.

Gabriel's real name is Joseph Junior Andreou O'Cearuill - but he is reported to have changed his name for commercial purposes.

In addition, United say they have provided Gabriel with first-team care and services - included regular meetings with senior coaches and nutritionists.

That he was included in the senior team photo is also viewed as further evidence of their commitment to his development and transition into first-team football.

When Gabriel committed himself to United in the summer of 2025, the lure of breaking through at United, and the targets he could aim for, was strong.

He was only 14 at the time but already he was looking towards the first team. Within a couple of months, Gabriel was called into senior training sessions by Ruben Amorim.

Expectation grew to such an extent that interim boss Darren Fletcher was asked if it was possible the forward could make his competitive bow in the FA Cup third-round tie with Brighton in January.

Fletcher - then Gabriel's coach at under-18 level - said no, believing the youngster wasn't physically ready.

However, as he continued to excel at under-18 level, it seemed a case of when, not if, Gabriel would be given his chance.

He ended the 2025-26 campaign as the Premier League's Under-18 player of the year and picked up the same award at United. It seemed certain he would be involved at the start of pre-season, when the majority of United's senior players would be absent after their World Cup exertions.

What happened instead solidified existing doubts of those close to Gabriel that United were the right club for him.

First, he was not part of Carrick's squad for the trip to Helsinki to face Wrexham in a friendly. On 24 July, he was an unused substitute against Rosenborg in Trondheim, a match in which Carrick made 10 outfield changes. Five of those players have since been sold or loaned out.

Gabriel finally got his chance against Atletico Madrid in Stockholm on 1 August, when he replaced Bryan Mbeumo for the final eight minutes.

That turned out to be it. He was on the bench for the final two games against Leeds and AC Milan, but did not get on. Against Leeds, former FA Youth Cup team-mate Dan Armer and 18-year-old newcomer Tynan Thompson were both introduced.

Doubts over Gabriel's physicality persisted, but his performances at under-21 level made a compelling argument he was ready.

Brighton was mentioned as a potential senior debut, but the perils around that made, for those close to Gabriel, the Champions League encounter with Sabah a better option.

The theory was correct. United beat them 4-0 and Carrick had used all five substitutes by the 72nd minute. The following week, United threw away a 2-0 lead and lost against Brighton.…

items.title: £800m in, £800m out - why Man City scandal shines light on Man Utd finances
items.content: <article>Manchester City's owners have been found guilty of injecting money into the club. At Manchester United, fans are frustrated at how much has been taken out.</article>
items.lbText:
The Premier League's statement laid it out in black and white.

'A total of £830.69m, payable and paid by Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) to the club'.

In other words, Manchester City 's owners circumvented the league's financial regulations by pumping money into the club.

The damning judgement landed less than five days after Manchester United 's extended filing to the New York Stock Exchange which detailed their end of year accounts to 30 June 2026.

Contained within it was an interest payment of £37m, an increase from £34m the previous year.

And respected football finance blogger Swiss Ramble now estimates that United's net interest payments since the leveraged Glazer takeover of the club in 2005 have risen to a total of £852m.

Without excusing City's owners in any way, it has not escaped the attentions of many fans from both Manchester clubs that while the arrival of one ownership group in the city has resulted in money being ploughed in, with the other, it has meant a similar significant sum being taken out.

United's latest accounts included this comment from chief executive Omar Berrada: "While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable."

This came after a third-place finish in the Premier League, which confirmed a return to the Champions League after a two-year absence.

Record revenues of £677.6m, projected to go as high as £760m in 2026-27, is something to celebrate.

Yet Berrada's cautious stance underlined a few home truths.

In confirming they had spent £191.7m on new players; notably Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, and costs associated with them, plus academy players such as England youth international Tynan Thompson, since 30 June, with payments due 'in the next five years'. United also revealed they had borrowed an additional £90m. It took their overall debt to £1.15bn.

To put that into context, in accounts to June 2021, the comparable sum was £667m.

Prior to 30 June, United's transfer debt was £375m. Of that, £218m must be paid before 30 June 2027. United have also said in addition to Baleba, Santos and Tielemans, they are liable for another £122.8m in potential contract payments if players they have already signed hit pre-agreed targets – although presumably the club would be happy if they ended up paying this.

When they restructured their debt in June, United added $125m (£94.36m) to their main debt. On 23 September, they said £63.5m had been spent on land for their proposed new stadium, the precise funding model for which is still to be determined.

Many fans, particularly those who do not want a new stadium, feel that money would have been better invested in Michael Carrick's squad.

Yet, as Berrada said, United are taking a 'disciplined approach' on that.

In 2025, United had the fifth highest wage bill in the Premier League, at £313m. The absence of European football means that sum dropped to £302m in 2025-26. No other clubs have released their figures yet, but it would be a major surprise if United climbed any higher, meaning Carrick over-achieved by finishing third. United's wages to turnover ratio is 45%. No club had a better figure than that last season.

While there are variables and also notable exceptions, including the Old Trafford outfit themselves who over the past decade, have topped the annual salary cost table but not the actual Premier League, and in 2024-25 finished 15th despite those fifth highest wage costs, there is a general correlation between salaries and performance.

Yet, while United were relatively restrained on the transfer front in terms of spending this summer – their £148m outlay was below that of newly-promoted Ipswich and Hull among others – their recent net spend has been high. The reason for this is clear.

When the most recent transfer window closed on 1 September, they had generated £47m from sales. It put them 11th in the Premier League. Only Liverpool of their 'big six' rivals brought in less.

Since they sold striker Romelu Lukaku to Inter Milan for £74m in 2019, United have only generated more than £25m for a player on four occasions – for Mason Greenwood, Scott McTominay, Rasmus Hojlund and Alejandro Garnacho.

It was instructive this summer a series of young players were sold, either for a lower fee than anticipated in the cases of Radek Vitek and Toby Collyer, who joined Middlesbrough and West Brom respectively, or none, like defenders Tyler Fredricson and James Overy. In all cases though, the transfers included significant sell-on and buy-back clauses, which is part of a strategy by United to generate more revenue from player sales.

In June 2023, Premier League clubs voted to cap future leveraged buyouts at around 65% of a club's value. The move seemed to be in response to ALK Capital's takeover of Burnley in December 2020.

Many United fans feel the move was 18 years too late.

The negativity around Manchester City 's scandal has indirectly, shone a light on the situation at Old Trafford.

Given there is little realistic chance of the substantive debt being paid off, Berrada and his colleagues must navigate the tricky balance of keeping costs under control, trimming the outstanding transfer fees, not extending the revolving credit limit and funding a new stadium – all while spending enough to deliver on the pitch.

In 2017-18, United made £80m in prize money from their run to the Champions League quarter-finals. In 2024-25, they got £31m for reaching the Europa League final. In their recently negotiated shirt deal with Adidas, a £10m annual reduction is applied if the club miss out on reaching the Champions League.

When Carrick sends his team out against bottom-club Tottenham at Old Trafford on 10 October, they will be attempting to drag themselves up from 12th place in the table.…

items.title: Ferguson 'terrified' before 'fantastic' return to Man Utd after brain haemorrhage
items.content: <article>Former Manchester United manager Sir Alex Ferguson speaks to BBC Breakfast as he approaches his 85th birthday.</article>
items.lbText:
"I was terrified," says Sir Alex Ferguson, one of the fiercest, most explosive and most decorated managers in football history.

The legendary former Manchester United boss is recalling the day he returned to Old Trafford for the first time after suffering a brain haemorrhage in May 2018.

Four months after emergency surgery, Ferguson - famous for his 'hairdryer treatment' when United dominated English football - was back to watch his beloved club take on Wolves in the Premier League.

The man responsible for making the dreams of United fans around the world come true for once was unsure of the reception he would receive from supporters.

"I wish I could say I was comfortable. I wasn't," Ferguson tells BBC Breakfast.

Ferguson and his wife Cathy received a standing ovation when they took their seats in the directors' box before kick-off.

"My wife was with me, and she was nearly crying," he said. "When we sat down, she said: 'That's fantastic.'"

Ferguson had been retired five years - after winning 38 trophies during 26 years in charge of United - at the time of his brain haemorrhage, aged 76.

Now three months short of 85, he says: "I'm feeling quite good despite small injuries."

The Scot has a new book coming out - 'Games of My Life'. It tells the stories of 21 defining matches in his playing and managerial career, revealing fresh insights into his journey from working-class Glasgow to dominating the English game - and Europe - as United boss.

Ferguson is thankful he is able to talk about the games that helped shape him.

"I had lost my voice; I couldn't speak," he says about the days immediately after brain surgery. "That was a frightening moment.

"I remember my grandsons coming to see me and I had lost my voice.

"Then they brought in a therapist and she started doing things like asking me to write down the names of birds, names of animals, names of rivers.

Unseen pictures in new Sir Alex Ferguson book detailing his favourite games

Ferguson won the lot during his time in charge of United between 1986 and 2013, including 13 Premier League titles.

He transformed them into a winning machine, and the history and tradition of United ran red through his veins.

As well as delivering two Champions League titles, Ferguson masterminded five FA Cup triumphs, won the League Cup four times and added the Club World Cup, European Super Cup, European Cup Winners' Cup and the Intercontinental Cup to the Old Trafford trophy cabinet.

In his book, Ferguson has picked standout games in his career, from winning his first cup final playing for Govan High School in Glasgow in 1955 at the age of 13 through to his retirement as a manager in 2013.

"That was my starting point," he says, holding the medal he received after that cup win 71 years ago.

"I played for Glasgow Schools, Scotland Schools and the Scotland youth team. The starting point of my career was there and I can look back with great satisfaction."

Ferguson describes growing up in Govan as "the making of me". He says he developed his inner confidence from his mother Elizabeth and a drive to succeed from his father Alexander, who worked in the Govan shipyards on the River Clyde.

"He was so proud of me and my brother," says Ferguson.

"He was a hard taskmaster because whenever I scored a hat-trick or a goal, my mother would say 'that's great, son'." His father, meanwhile, offered tough constructive criticism however many goals Ferguson had scored.

After making his debut as a 16-year-old striker for Queen's Park, Ferguson ended up at St Johnstone, where he endured a frustrating spell and nearly quit football for a new life in Canada.

"I wasn't enjoying it. I wasn't playing first-team football; I was in the reserves all the time," he says.

"I filled out all the forms and phoned my aunt in Canada, because you needed a sponsor then, and never told my mother and father."

The next day St Johnstone, decimated by a flu bug in the team, arrived at Ibrox to take on Rangers. A 21-year-old Ferguson was promoted to the starting XI and scored a hat-trick.

That life-changing performance in 1963 revived his playing career and set him on the path to becoming one of football's greatest managers.

"I would say this to young people - don't miss the biggest opportunity in your life. It's recognising it."

Ferguson is sat in front of a table for the interview, which was conducted before the Premier League announced on Tuesday that Manchester City had been found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of financial regulations between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

On the table are several items from his career, including the Scotland cap he was finally presented with in 2021 - 54 years after appearing for his country.

Ferguson received the cap at Hampden Park on the night Scott McTominay - then a United player - scored a dramatic stoppage-time winner in a 3-2 win over Israel in a World Cup qualifier.

"I remember signing McTominay at seven years of age," Ferguson says.

Also on the table are old letters addressed to Ferguson from disgruntled United fans amid speculation he was about to sell midfielder Paul Ince to Inter Milan in the summer of 1995.

One reads: 'Don't sell Incey to Inter - or you'll regret it'. Another reads: 'Every Red is disgusted with you'.

"Paul was a tremendous footballer, there's no doubt about that," says Ferguson.

"He had incredible ability, but I just had that feeling that he just got carried away a bit at the time.

"He then got this offer from Inter Milan. I'm trying to weigh up one thing against the other. I'm looking at Paul Scholes and I said 'should we?'

"Milan's offer went from £7m to £7.5m and I said 'do it'.

"That's what your job is as a manager. You have to make hard decisions, and some decisions don't suit everyone."

There is also a notebook on the table with a list of words scribbled down by Ferguson when he used to address his players.…

items.title: Man Utd and Arsenal wins among 'best in Brighton's history'
items.content: <article>Tony Bloom helped transform the club's fortunes after he became majority shareholder in 2009.</article>
items.lbText:
Brighton & Hove Albion owner Tony Bloom says he is looking forward to seeing what the Seagulls can achieve after results he described as the "best in the history of the football club".

In a rare interview, Bloom told BBC South East victory over Manchester United in the Carabao Cup, a 3-0 win over champions Arsenal, and the 5-0 thrashing of Coventry City had boosted confidence at the club.

Bloom helped transform Brighton's fortunes after he became majority shareholder at the club in 2009, when the team were struggling in the third tier of English football and playing at a temporary ground.

"(I'm) looking forward to what this team can achieve this season", Bloom said.

The Seagulls are currently third in the Premier League and are tipped to win the Europa Conference League.

Bloom's grandfather Harry was vice-chairman at the club in the 1970s, and he's been a fan since childhood.

He would watch them play at the Goldstone Ground, which Brighton were forced to leave due to debt in 1997.

The club were promoted to the Premier League eight years after he took control and celebrated its 125 -year anniversary at the victory over Arsenal on 19 September.

That win was three days after coming back from 2-0 down to knock Manchester United out of the League Cup at Old Trafford, and they beat Coventry the weekend before.

Bloom's leadership and sustainable business model - buying and selling players at a huge profit with a data-led approach - has become the envy of clubs worldwide.

Brighton, however, have not won silverware since promotion, and Bloom doesn't dwell on their successes so far.

"It's vital that we always look forward, there's no point in looking back," he said.

"We're always looking to improve in everything we do in terms of performances, in terms of results, processes, innovative way of doing things because our competition is doing the same so if you stand still you go backwards.

"So we enjoy the moments and then move on because we have to keep improving."

Brighton are about to start their second ever European campaign, this time in the Conference League, a cup that rivals Crystal Palace won last season.

"Obviously, winning leagues, winning trophies is really difficult, but I do think we've got a real chance," Bloom said.

"The Conference League is a very winnable tournament compared to others we've played in."

Bloom said he also hoped Brighton's women's side would win a trophy this season.

Having bankrolled the building of Brighton's Amex Stadium, he said he is now "really excited" about the club's plans for a new £80m women's stadium .

He added: "Having a stadium right next to the Amex is perfect for us."

"I'm really looking forward to 2030 when hopefully the players will be walking out at our new stadium."

Brighton plan Europe's first purpose-built £80m women's stadium

'Supporting the Albion has been a rollercoaster'

From the brink of extinction to Europa League

items.title: Fernandes, Gakpo & Dorgu join injury list
items.content: <article>Bruno Fernandes, Cody Gakpo and Patrick Dorgu all join the international break's high-profile injury list after suffering issues that have curtailed their involvement in Nations League matches.</article>
items.lbText:
Bruno Fernandes, Cody Gakpo and Patrick Dorgu have all joined the international break's high-profile injury list after suffering issues that have curtailed their involvement in Nations League matches.

After playing in Portugal's win over Wales on Thursday, Manchester United captain Fernandes was not in the squad for Sunday's fixture against Norway.

Prior to the match boss Jorge Jesus revealed , external Fernandes had "played through the pain" against Wales and "wasn't his usual self".

"He played with an injury he brought from Manchester United ," he said. "He really wanted to play against Wales."

Meanwhile, both Fernandes' United team-mate Dorgu and Liverpool striker Gakpo suffered injuries during games for their respective countries on Sunday.

Gakpo had to go off just 17 minutes into the Netherlands' 2-1 win against Serbia, grimacing and holding the lower part of his right leg.

Liverpool confirmed on Thursday that the Dutchman had returned to the club after withdrawing from Netherlands' squad.

"It's his ankle, that's all I know," Netherlands boss Xavi said on Sunday. "Tomorrow we will know, but hopefully it's not too important."

Dorgu, meanwhile, lasted 30 minutes before he limped off in Denmark's 2-0 win against Wales and is set to return to Manchester for further investigations on a suspected hamstring problem.

The first international break of the 2026-27 men's football season is lasting a week longer than it usually does, with the traditional October break now scrapped.

There is now a three-week gap for international fixtures across late September and early October, where countries will play four international matches instead of two.

Injured Isak returns to Liverpool from Sweden duty

Why will September international break last three weeks?

Gakpo's injury adds to Liverpool 's woes after Alexander Isak withdrew from Sweden duty with a minor thigh injury.

The striker played the full 90 minutes and scored a goal in his side's 2-1 win on Friday over Romania in the Nations League.

However, he will not be involved in Sweden's remaining three matches in this international break and assessed by his club's medical staff.

On Thursday, Arsenal forward Kai Havertz and Sunderland 's Brian Brobbey both went off injured in the same game as the Netherlands drew with Germany.

German Havertz was caught on the knee by a high boot from Quinten Timber in Amsterdam and had to be replaced.

Netherlands forward Brobbey - off the back off a hat-trick in Sunderland 's 5-3 Premier League defeat by Manchester City - then appeared to suffer a muscle injury.

A further blow for Sunderland on this international break came as Dan Ballard suffered a hamstring injury late in Northern Ireland's 1-0 win over Georgia on Friday.

Boss Michael O'Neill has confirmed the injury will rule him out of the national team's remaining fixtures in this international break.

It is not just Premier League teams who are being impacted by injuries to their players while on international duty.

Real Madrid striker Kylian Mbappe has been ruled out for at least two weeks after injuring his knee while scoring the winner in Zinedine Zidane's first game in charge of France.

He scored a record-extending 67th goal from Michael Olise's pass to sink Turkey, but he was limping immediately and had to be replaced five minutes later.

Meanwhile, Bayern Munich's Jamal Musiala suffered a muscle injury during the warm-up for the game against the Netherlands and had to withdraw.

items.title: Sporting Witness
items.content: <article>Magi Haroun was the first female photographer in the Premier League</article>
items.lbText:
Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK.

Find out how to listen to other BBC stations

World Service , · 26 Sep 2026 , · 10 mins

In the 1990s Magi Haroun became the first female football photographer in the Premier League. She had begun her career in footballing photography in 1986 after growing up with close connections to Manchester United. Her uncle was the club’s chairman from 1965 until 1980, and she had a good relationship with Sir Alex Ferguson during his tenure as manager. She spoke to Tim O’Callaghan in 2025 about embarking on a career in a male-dominated field. She also revealed the unlikely story of how she rescued a cat from Manchester United’s training ground. Eye-witness accounts brought to life by archive and testimony. Sporting Witness is for those fascinated by sporting history. We take you to the events that have shaped the sports world through the eyes of the people who were there. For nine minutes, you become a fan in the stands as we take you back in time to examine memorable victories and agonising defeats from all over the world. You’ll hear from people who have achieved sporting immortality, or those who were there as incredible sporting moments unfolded. Recent episodes explore the forgotten football Women’s World Cup, the plasterer who fought a boxing legend, international football’s biggest ever beating and the man who swam the Amazon river. We look at the lives of some of the most famous F1 drivers, tennis players and athletes as well as people who’ve had ground-breaking impact in their chosen sporting field, including: the most decorated Paralympian, the woman who was the number 1 squash player in the world for nine years, and the first figure skater to wear a hijab. You can learn all about fascinating and surprising stories, such as the tennis player who escaped the Nazis, how a man finally beat a horse in a race, and how the FIFA computer game was created. (Photo: Magi at work. Credit: Handout via Magi Haroun)

items.title: Why schoolboys have become a huge part of football's transfer market
items.content: <article>BBC Sport explores why clubs at the top of English football are increasingly trading academy players and what the impact is on the youngsters themselves.</article>
items.lbText:
A 15-year-old growing up in the UK faces many tough personal decisions about their future - which school subjects to study, which social circle suits them, and where their priorities lie in life.

But in the past few weeks the choices teenage Manchester United striker JJ Gabriel has been making about his future in football have drawn huge public attention in sports media and online.

Gabriel has informed United he wants to leave the club and join another. BBC Sport has reported that he has stayed away from training and begun talking to other clubs because he and his representatives are unhappy with United's handling of the 15-year-old's progress.

That a transfer saga involving a footballer so young could generate so much interest highlights a truth that to many is uncomfortable - money is changing how the football transfer market works, and children are increasingly deemed to be among its most valuable commodities.

So what is behind the rise in transfers involving boys who in some cases are not even old enough to have taken their GCSEs, what kind of influence can the money on offer have on agents and parents, and what exactly are the country's top football clubs getting out of it?

"It's crazy when you think about it," says Ryan Cardwell, former youth scout at Liverpool and Southampton.

"In what other kind of world would 15 and 16-year-olds be spoken about in the media like this?"

This summer alone, all six of the Premier League's wealthiest clubs either signed a highly-rated academy player from another, or lost a youngster to a direct rival.

"It is such a competitive market," Cardwell explains. "There are now tens of transfers between the elite academies every summer, when it used to be the case that if you were already at one of those, you would likely stay the course.

"The race for talent is huge – you look at what teams are spending on transfers for senior players and it's enormous, so if you can spot a player earlier and offset some of that financial risk, you're going to do so."

Some inside football claim that the transfer of Rio Ngumoha - the now 18-year-old winger who was called up to this month's senior England squad - from Chelsea to Liverpool at the age of 15 in 2024 ushered in a new era of competition for academy players among the nation's elite.

One of the major factors is Brexit. Before 2021 English clubs were allowed to sign academy players over the age of 16 who held European Union passports.

Since the UK left the EU, foreign players cannot join English clubs until they reach 18.

"Heathrow and Gatwick [airports] on a Friday night were inundated with scouts going to other countries to look for young players", says Cardwell.

"Belgium and the Netherlands were full of scouts for Premier League clubs.

"Now it's the competition between English clubs that has increased, looking at each other's players, including the old-school 'top six' but also the likes of Southampton, Aston Villa , and Fulham ."

Young players have further added financial value - youth signings don't count towards the Premier League's squad cost ratio rules, and any future sale counts as 'pure profit' in club accounts.

Advances in video technology and data analysis mean more young players are being identified, tracked and approached by rival clubs than ever before.

Players can de-register from their academy at the end of their under-12, under-14 and under-16 seasons if they wish to explore options elsewhere.

They can be offered paid scholarship contracts from the season in which they turn 14, and can sign professional deals from the season in which they turn 16.

Some pundits and fans have criticised Gabriel's family over the controversy in recent weeks.

Gabriel can potentially join clubs in Europe because he has an Irish passport.

"It's a really tough world - players and families want the best for their kids and you can't give them stick without knowing what their motivations are," says Phil Jagielka, whose son Zac left Liverpool in 2024 and signed a scholarship deal at Hull City at 16.

"The harsh reality is that if a young player fails to progress, or gets a bad injury, teams will stop being interested in them. So there is an element of strike while the iron's hot."

When a club signs a player from a rival academy, they pay a set compensation fee based on how long they had been trained there.

Depending on the player's age, the fee can reach millions of pounds.

The increasing allure of signing young academy players from rivals means some parents are now compiling data packs on their sons to give to potential clubs, and more and more children are represented by football agents.

"There are good agents and bad agents," Cardwell says.

"You certainly speak to some and think 'that's completely the wrong idea', or, ' this player is going to be misguided'. Sometimes they push for a move when a player isn't ready.

"The contracts can be enormous and [money] can be a huge motivation to move. It could set a young player's family up for life.

"I would quite like to see some form of financial cap. My fear for some of the young players is they're on the biggest salaries they'll ever have, because if they don't make it at the top level, they can go from being on tens of thousands (of pounds) a week to one or two thousand lower down the pyramid."

In decades gone by, development of academy players would be combined with menial tasks around the training ground.

The idea was to keep young footballers grounded and make them feel a part of the wider club.

But the Gabriel case demonstrates the significant changes football has undergone.

"We would clean boots, sweep floors, tidy the changing rooms," says Jagielka, who came through Sheffield United's academy in the late 1990s.

"I fully back that system. It taught us responsibility and discipline. It was a way of getting to know the first-team players, and you would get a proper telling off if you didn't do your jobs properly.…

items.title: Man Utd borrow another £90m as debt tops £1.1bn
items.content: <article>Manchester United confirm they have borrowed another £90m since 30 June, to take their overall debt to more than £1.1bn.</article>
items.lbText:
Manchester United have borrowed another £90m since 30 June - and confirmed they spent £191.7m on new players this summer.

United bought Andrey Santos from Chelsea on 13 July, Youri Tielemans from Aston Villa on 14 July and Carlos Baleba from Brighton on 25 August.

The fees the club stated they spent on the trio at the time the transfers were announced added up to £153m, and it is not clear where the additional sum has been spent.

The club have been approached for comment.

Confirmation of the additional borrowing of £90m was included in a more detailed filing to the New York Stock Exchange on Thursday, following Wednesday's release of their 2025-26 accounts to 30 June, and showed their overall debt was still more than £1bn despite major cost-cutting measures implemented by Sir Jim Ratcliffe since he became minority owner in 2024.

United confirmed it made three further drawdowns from its revolving credit limit, on 29 and 31 July and 28 August, totalling £120m. It then paid back £30m on 21 September.

It takes United's overall debt to £1.15bn, made up of the historic debt, which now stands at £578m, the £200m outstanding on its revolving credit facility, and £375m in outstanding transfer fees.

That is a £72m reduction on the £447m they stated was owed in transfer fees in the 2024-25 accounts. However, it remains a large sum, with £104.8m due in between one and two years and £51.9m in between two and five years - with the remainder due in the next 12 months.

The club say payments for their most recent transfers "are due within the next five years".

items.title: Barcelona's Deco denies interest in Man Utd's Gabriel
items.content: <article>Barcelona sporting director Deco says the club is not interested in Manchester United teenager JJ Gabriel.</article>
items.lbText:
Barcelona's sporting director Deco said the club has no interest in pursuing Manchester United teenager JJ Gabriel.

Gabriel, 15, travelled to the Spanish city after informing United that he wanted to leave Old Trafford earlier this month.

Real Madrid, Bayern Munich and Paris St-Germain are among the clubs reportedly keen on securing his signature.

"There's nothing to say about this boy," Deco said at a news conference.

"It's normal we always have players linked with us. There's a huge market for that, even when they are young.

"We are not interested in any player in his situation. I'm not sure what's happening, and if he's still a Manchester United player. We are not involved in that.

"First of all, we need to understand how the situation is before we try to do something. To speak about young, teenage players, it is not our business."

Gabriel has not trained at United since scoring a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut on 10 September.

Tournament rules prevent him from playing for a side other than United in this season's competition.

But if he obtains a European Union passport through either his father - a former Republic of Ireland international - or mother, who has Greek-Cypriot heritage, he could join a club in the EU when he turns 16 on 6 October.

Last week, United manager Michael Carrick urged for people to be "careful and sensible" about the amount of exposure and scrutiny given to the youngster.

items.lbText:
Manchester United are selling pieces of their Old Trafford pitch for £125 each.

The initiative was announced the same day that the club reported that overall debt remains more than £1bn.

The first batch put on sale has already sold out.

While United recorded a record revenue of £677.6m and a £22.6m operating profit for 2025-26, they had a pre-tax loss of £43m.

The 13-time Premier League champions also confirmed £63.5m had been spent on buying land for the team's new stadium, which is expected to cost more than £2bn overall.

For the first time in 14 years, the Old Trafford pitch was dug up this summer and stripped back to its foundation.

Sections of the turf were preserved, with pieces measuring 7x7cm then being placed in glass cubes.

The cubes are presented inside a black case.

The club website says that the cubes make a "priceless memento of iconic games played at home and keeps the memories of matchdays alive".

items.title: When Bellamy watched on as Ronaldo caused lockdown
items.content: <article>Craig Bellamy says Cristiano Ronaldo is "beyond a superstar" before his Wales side face the Portugal legend in the opening match of their Nations League A campaign.</article>
items.lbText:
With five Ballon d'Or wins, eight league titles, five Champions Leagues, a European Championship and a pair of Nations League triumphs among his glut of honours, Cristiano Ronaldo's status as one of football's all-time greats is not in doubt.

But a chance encounter with the Portugal legend helped Wales boss Craig Bellamy appreciate that the 41-year-old is significantly more than just a footballing icon.

Bellamy was on a pre-season trip to Lisbon during his time as an assistant to manager Vincent Kompany at Burnley when the Portuguese capital's airport was effectively put into lockdown.

It led to the Welshman describing Ronaldo as "beyond a superstar" after he realised the vast presence of police and security officials were to help escort the global icon.

"So we got to the airport and the police were everywhere. It was on lockdown," Bellamy said.

Ronaldo spurred on by 1,000 goals and Portugal glory

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC One Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

"We're Burnley and we had a little bit of VIP. We were on a coach, we were chartered but still had to go into the airport a certain way.

"It was like rows of police with police cars everywhere. We thought, 'something has happened, there must be a warning here'.

"Everything was locked off. People in the terminal, you name it. We couldn't get off the coach and we had to wait for what we thought was a security breach or something.

"We are stuck on the coach for 10, 15 minutes and suddenly this car turns up, it parks and a guy walks out, goes in the boot, grabs a rucksack and someone else gets out and puts the rucksack on and who is it? Ronaldo."

Bellamy added: "He is walking on his own with police everywhere and Lisbon airport locked off. Even the police were taking pictures. No-one could bother him.

"It was the coolest walk I have ever watched for a minute.

"We were all on the coach and our jaws dropped. Everyone who had been moaning quickly shut up. It was like presidents stuff."

Bellamy last shared a pitch with Ronaldo in October 2008 as the Portuguese scored twice for Manchester United in a 2-0 Premier League win over West Ham United at Old Trafford.

He is now set to manage his country against the 233-cap international as Wales kick-start their Nations League A campaign in Portugal on Thursday night.

As he bids to conjure up a plan to nullify Ronaldo and the rest of the star-studded Portugal squad at the Estadio Jose Alvalade, Bellamy was eager to fully reflect on the experience of the forward he witnessed at Lisbon airport.

"How can you lock off a whole airport?" added Bellamy.

"I would not be able to get my computer through customs in Cardiff airport. What have I just seen?

"The reason I'm telling the story is because that's how big this guy is.

"It was like, 'wow'. I'm so glad I saw that moment because he is beyond a superstar."

What will 'greatest captain' bring to Bellamy's Wales?

FAW chief questions Infantino's Fifa reform claims

During the summer, Ronaldo confirmed the 2026 World Cup would be his last.

However, the Al-Nassr frontman has so far not revealed when he will finally bring his glittering career to an end.

Despite the uncertainty surrounding Ronaldo's future, Bellamy says he can fully understand why the forward - now in his 24th year as a senior Portugal international - is still operating at an elite level.

"I'm not surprised he is still playing with the professionalism he has shown," added Bellamy.

"It's also how clever he is, he knows how to protect himself, he knows not to waste his energy at certain times and he's still got the habit of goal-scoring, and you never lose that.

"We're talking about not just one of the greatest players of our generation, we're talking all generations with what he has been able to do. He's beyond a superstar."

Inside the Wales camp: Jordan James & Connor Roberts

For all of the spotlight on Ronaldo and his team-mates, Bellamy knows his full focus - along with that of his players and staff - must be on how Wales can leave the City of Light with a positive result.

The head coach's already tough task has been made harder by the fact he will be without players including Harry Wilson, Joe Rodon, Karl Darlow, Nathan Broadhead, Dylan Lawlor, Rubin Colwill and Isaak Davies in Lisbon.

But Bellamy has urged his players to show the right kind of fight as they bid to upset the odds and remain in the top tier of the Nations League over the coming months.

"We have to be excited, but not too excited," he added.

"We have worked hard to get into League A, so what can we do to stay in it? If we do then it will help us massively and that's the motivation.

"You want to be in these moments. I'm telling you, when your playing days finish, you won't remember Bury away and all that. These moments you will remember and will live with you.

"But you also want to remember how you performed. You don't want this to get too much.

"I want my players to go out and give everything. They should love every second of it. That's the drive for this."

items.title: Man Utd still £1bn in debt with £63.5m spent on new stadium
items.content: <article>Manchester United's overall debt remains over £1bn despite Sir Jim Ratcliffe's extensive cost-cutting measures, with the club also confirming it has spent £63.5m buying land for their new stadium.</article>
items.lbText:
Manchester United's overall debt remains over £1bn despite Sir Jim Ratcliffe's extensive cost-cutting measures, with the club also confirming it has spent £63.5m buying land for the team's new stadium.

Amid a backdrop of fan protests and a disappointing start to the season that has left United 12th in the Premier League and already out of the EFL Cup, the club have announced record revenues of £677.6m and a £22.6m operating profit despite not playing in Europe for the first time in a decade.

This represents a huge shift from the £113.2m loss in 2023-24.

However, while United have saved £8.5m of a projected £16.5m pay-off to axed boss Ruben Amorim after he accepted a job at AC Milan, other costs have increased.

Net finance costs for the year were £69.6m, an increase of 228.3%. United put most of this down to a foreign exchange loss. According to football finance expert Kieran Maguire, net finance costs alone have now exceeded £1bn since the leveraged Glazer family buyout in 2005.

In addition, United also confirmed they spent £63.5m of an additional $125m (£94.14m) added to their historic debt during a summer refinancing move on land for their new stadium. The club have not explained what they have done with the remainder. The stadium itself is likely to cost in excess of £2bn.

It means the club's overall debt, while reducing from £1.3bn at the end of December, is still over £1bn, made up of the historic debt, which now stands at £577.6m, the £111.4m outstanding on its revolving credit facility, and outstanding transfer fees, which club sources say represents approximately 75% of the £473m listed and being owed as 'trade and other payables'.

This comes at a time when supporters are furious about what they believe to be chronic under investment in Michael Carrick's first-team squad this summer.

United spent £148m on three new signings - Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans. It was less than a third of the £458m Manchester City invested in their squad and lower even than promoted Ipswich.

However, fans are angry there was no additional left-back purchased to provide competition for Luke Shaw, who has missed three matches because of injury already, or striking support for Benjamin Sesko, who missed pre-season as he recovered from a shin complaint that has already resurfaced.

While United argue the additional funds were earmarked for their stadium, to be built 350 yards away from where Old Trafford stands, the loan itself is lodged within club accounts.

"We are pleased to have secured record revenues," said chief executive Omar Berrada.

"This demonstrates the underlying strength of our business, and shows the direct impact of the work we have been doing over the past two years.

"While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable.

"With that financial sustainability in mind, we have strengthened both our men's and women's teams during the summer window and our men's team has seen the return of Champions League football to Old Trafford."

United have also been criticised for a lack of investment in the Women's Super League squad, who currently sit second bottom of the table with one point from three games.

Ratcliffe previously argued the club had to take strong action to slash losses. Two lots of redundancies led to 450 people losing their jobs, while United have confirmed their latest set of salary costs have reduced by £11.3m to £302m.

"This is primarily due to changes in the make-up of the men's first-team squad, combined with savings associated with headcount reduction programs implemented over the previous two fiscal years," said the club.

items.title: Was Neville right to call out Man Utd for a 'lack of effort'?
items.content: <article>The former Manchester United full-back said a 15-minute period in the 1-1 draw at Fulham was the "worst I've ever seen" - do the stats back him up and does his media portfolio amplify the noise? </article>
items.lbText:
"I've watched Manchester United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen. Absolutely pathetic."

Gary Neville did not hold back in his criticism of Manchester United's performance during Sky Sports' coverage of Sunday's 1-1 draw at Fulham .

The players had just laboured through the opening stages of the second half, culminating in a Lisandro Martinez own goal gifting the home side the lead.

"I've never seen such a lack of effort," Neville added. "What must Michael Carrick be thinking?"

Neville played 602 games for United over a 19-year career, winning everything the club game had to offer. So his criticism comes from a qualified position.

This season's out-of-possession stats would appear to back it up too, with the Red Devils ranking 16th for distance covered, and 17th for total number of sprints.

How did United play under Carrick when they were winning games towards the end of last season?

And, as Neville makes the headlines, what does this say about his influence in the media around Manchester United?

United's dismal running and sprinting stats made for stark reading in the wake of Neville's criticism.

After all, the former right-back had directly questioned a lack of effort, and referred to the players as "mannequins".

He said United - and Fulham - were walking too much during the game.

In the Premier League this season only four teams have covered less distance than the Red Devils, and just three teams have produced fewer sprints.

It comes alongside United's joint-worst start to a Premier League season, with four points from five games.

So is this down to the running and the effort?

Let's take a look at the second half of last season, after Carrick had been appointed as manager.

Between 17 January and the end of the season, United picked up more points than any other team - 39 points from 17 games.

Yet only four teams ran less than United, and only two clubs had fewer sprints.

There is no material difference in the running stats, but United were returning 2.29 points per game compared to the 0.8 this season.

Something is clearly different, but it does not appear to be linked to this particular stat because barely anything has changed - apart from the results. Maybe this United squad simply does not have runners.

Then there is the comparison to rival teams.

Manchester City have won all five Premier League matches but have covered less distance than United. Enzo Maresca's squad have also recorded the lowest number of sprints in the division.

Brighton, one of the most exciting teams in the league this season and the top goalscorers, are one place above United for sprints.

Maybe United's problem is tactical rather than a simple case of not running enough?

Neville setting the media agenda when it comes to United is not a new thing.

The former England international has called out the team's shortcomings on many occasions.

Look back to December 2021, and a poor first-half performance against a struggling Newcastle side when Ralf Rangnick's side trailed 1-0 at the break.

"They're a bunch of whinge-bags," Neville said at half-time on Sky Sports. "I'll not go into names but they're whinging at each other, arms up in the air complaining about everything.

"There's no pressing, no urgency, the basics of the game."

Edinson Cavani rescued a point at St James' Park, but Neville's comments had already made the headlines.

You only need to look at how the post-match coverage went after the Fulham draw.

Neville's remarks were put to Carrick at full-time. The United manager said fitness levels of his players were not an issue.

"Neville: That was the worst ever", read the back page of Monday's Daily Telegraph.

"15 minutes of shame", was the lead for the sports section of the Daily Star.

"United boss keeps calm after Neville Ful blast," said the Daily Express.

It was picked up across online media, and discussed at length on radio talk shows - including across the BBC, as evidenced by this piece.

When Neville criticises his former club, it carries weight.

In January, with Ruben Amorim under pressure for poor results, the Portuguese head coach said that "if people cannot handle the Gary Nevilles and the criticisms of everything, we need to change the club".

There always seems to be a strong influence in the media related to the dominant team of a previous era.

For example, throughout the 1990s and 2000s, former Liverpool stars such as Alan Hansen, Mark Lawrenson and Phil Thompson dominated a lot of the conversation.

It stands to reason that now members of the all-conquering United squad will have a leading role in the media.

But for Neville, it is bigger than anyone apart from Gary Lineker and his Goalhanger production company.

How Lineker and Neville became rival media moguls

Neville calls Man Utd 'pathetic' - but Carrick maintains belief

'I've asked for forgiveness' - Eckert and Southampton braced for Spygate verdict

"When does Sky wonder if they are paying a lot of money in wages to train their next competitor?"

It is a question posed by Richard Gillis, who hosts the Unofficial Partner sports business podcast.

While Neville started out in the media as a pundit with Sky Sports, the 51-year-old is now one of the biggest players in a rapidly changing industry.

After co-founding the sports entertainment production company Buzz16 in 2016, Neville launched YouTube platform The Overlap in 2021.

The Overlap produces Stick to Football - one of the UK's most popular football content channels with 2.2 billion views across all platforms in 2025.

Earlier this year it entered into a strategic partnership with radio giants Global, with the aim to create a multi-format sports media network.

Neville this summer exited Buzz16, focusing his attention on The Overlap, which has branched out into cricket and rugby, and secured live Bundesliga rights.…

items.title: Wilson, Darlow and Broadhead out of Wales squad
items.content: <article>Wales suffer a triple blow before their Nations League A campaign with Harry Wilson, Nathan Broadhead and Karl Darlow all out of Craig Bellamy's squad.</article>
items.lbText:
Wales have suffered a triple blow before their Nations League A campaign with Harry Wilson, Nathan Broadhead and Karl Darlow pulling out of Craig Bellamy's squad.

Leeds attacking midfielder Wilson - Wales' most influential player in recent times - had been a doubt with a quad problem while Wrexham forward Broadhead was expected to miss out due to a thigh issue.

First-choice goalkeeper Darlow has also withdrawn despite making his Manchester United debut in the EFL Cup last week and being on the bench for the Red Devils' Premier League draw with Fulham on Sunday.

Wales have called up veteran Leicester City keeper David Cornell and Huddersfield Town forward Joe Taylor - both of whom are uncapped - as well as Reading midfielder Charlie Savage as replacements.

Bellamy's team face Portugal in their Nations League opener in Lisbon on Thursday before they meet Denmark in Copenhagen next Sunday.

They then take on Norway in Cardiff on Thursday, 1 October before the Danes visit the Welsh capital three days later.

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC One Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

Wales were already without key defenders Joe Rodon and Dylan Lawlor, while Cardiff City duo Rubin Colwill and Isaak Davies are also unavailable.

Cornell, 35, joined Leicester on a one-year deal last Friday having been a free agent after leaving Preston North End in the summer.

The former Wales Under-21 international, from Swansea, has made more than 200 senior club appearances having played for a string of clubs since coming through Swansea City's academy.

Taylor, another former Wales Under-21 player, has scored five goals for Huddersfield so far this season.

The Peterborough-born 23-year-old shone while on loan at Wigan Athletic in the second half of the last campaign having previously impressed at Lincoln City and Colchester United.

Savage, the son of former Wales midfielder Robbie, is a regular at Reading, where he has made more than 150 appearances since joining from Manchester United in 2023.

items.title: Will three-week break put more pressure on managers?
items.content: <article>So far this season three coaches have lost their jobs, but plenty of others will be looking over their shoulders heading into the new, extended international break.</article>
items.lbText:
Three weeks is a long time in football - especially if you are a manager struggling for results.

So far this season three EFL coaches have lost their jobs - Paul Heckingbottom at Preston North End, Michael Duff at Wycombe Wanderers and Peterborough's Luke Williams.

But plenty of others will be looking over their shoulders as the new, extended international break begins.

Take Manchester United manager Michael Carrick, who has endured the club's joint-worst start to a Premier League season with four points from five games.

His side were also eliminated from the EFL Cup in midweek despite leading 2-0 against Brighton . It was the first time in 50 years the Red Devils had lost at home after being two goals up.

United then drew 1-1 at Fulham on Sunday, which extended the Cottagers' winless league run this term - so pressure is also building on their boss Alvaro Arbeloa.

Rock bottom of the Premier League table are Tottenham Hotspur . Roberto de Zerbi needs results, and fast.

Next up after the international break? Manchester United v Tottenham .

They are not the only managers who might have cause for concern. But is this international break really the right time to make changes?

'Not a catastrophe' - Carrick dismisses Man Utd job fears

No revival in sight for 'fragile' Spurs after Villa defeat

Analysis: Hosts winless but showing signs of growth

Over the past 10 years, it has been rare for a Premier League manager to be replaced this early in the campaign.

Even more so during the international break.

But could it be different this year? This first break is longer - three weeks rather than two - and comes later.

The September slot used to come at the start of the month when clubs had only played three league fixtures.

In the past 10 years, only two managers - Watford's Javi Gracia in 2019 and Nottingham Forest 's Nuno Espirito Santo last year - moved on during this break.

What about the October stoppage? Again, only two managers have previously lost their jobs during the same period - Francesco Guidolin at Swansea in 2016, and Xisco Munoz at Watford in 2021.

This suggests clubs do not tend to use an international break to change manager.

It is, though, far more likely to happen in November, with six bosses replaced in the past 10 years.

That does not mean managers are safe, though. The changes simply were not made during the breaks.

In the past 10 campaigns, nine coaches had left their jobs by the time the second international break came along - which is roughly where we are in the number of games.

So could some clubs opt for a change in the next three weeks?

Former Stoke, West Brom and Middlesbrough boss Tony Pulis explains when the pressure can build for a football manager.

With the first international break upon us, rumblings around certain clubs that have started the season poorly have surfaced.

In my time, the October/November international breaks, the pause just after the Christmas period, and then early March would be the three sticking points for any manager who was struggling with results.

Why these breaks are used for clubs to make changes is plain to see. The pause in the season gives football clubs the chance to appoint a new manager with time for them to settle into their new role, to take stock of the surroundings, staff and time to prepare for their first game in charge.

After Christmas, usually the first game is an FA Cup match, which again gives the new boss a chance close up to see what they have to work with. First impressions can be a vital starting point, so again the manager has time to prepare and deliver their principles to the lads.

Personally, I've joined quite a few of my clubs midway through seasons, and have left a few clubs going the other way, but I do honestly believe that those international breaks, for the reasons I've given, definitely heighten the chances of struggling managers getting the sack.

I don't see this September break as a flashing light, it is too early in the season, but from then on in, the dates I have mentioned really do come into play.

But this early international break doesn't help any managers.

Whether your team is winning or losing, on both accounts, it's a nightmare. If you're winning you want to keep playing, and yet if you've started badly as a manager you want more time to put it right. Players travelling and the chance of injuries at such an early stage of the season is completely bonkers in my opinion.

While the evidence suggests things have to get pretty bad for a club to change manager early in the season, a few bosses are feeling the heat.

Despite the disappointment of losing to Brighton in midweek, I did not see the trip to Fulham as having been 'make or break' for Carrick in the sense of his job.

Carrick himself said it would have been "ridiculous" to think that way - and I agree.

He got enough credit in the bank last season by steering United into the Champions League to ride out a poor start to this campaign.

I think the issue is United generate so much debate that a draw at Craven Cottage against a team that had only one point, and was bottom of the table, was always going to lead to numerous external inquests.

And in turn it puts a laser focus on United when they resume their campaign against Tottenham on 10 October.

It is unclear exactly how much danger Arbeloa is in, but there appears to be some substance to reports of disgruntlement among elements of Fulham 's squad early in the campaign.

His significant tactical changes since replacing Marco Silva have left the Cottagers vulnerable at the back, although they were more solid in a goalless draw at Liverpool last weekend and in Sunday's draw with United.

Silva spent five years at Craven Cottage, but Fulham owner Shahid Khan has shown a ruthless streak in the past when making managerial changes.…

items.title: Neville calls Man Utd 'pathetic' - but Carrick maintains belief
items.content: <article>Gary Neville calls Manchester United "pathetic", but boss Michael Carrick maintains belief after salvaging draw at Fulham.</article>
items.lbText:
Gary Neville took a deep breath after Lisandro Martinez's own goal put Fulham ahead just over an hour into what had been a laboured Manchester United performance, and delivered his verdict.

The former United skipper is never short of a scathing word, but even by his standards, this was brutal.

"I've watched Manchester United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen," he said. "Absolutely pathetic.

"I've never seen such a lack of effort. What must [Michael] Carrick be thinking?"

For context, Neville was part of the United side beaten 3-1 by Sunday's opponents Fulham at Old Trafford in October 2003 . In recent memory they have also lost 7-0 at Liverpool and 6-1 at home twice, to Tottenham and Manchester City.

Neville's words came after a poor quarter of an hour from the start of the second half to Martinez's moment of ill fortune, before United went on to snatch a 1-1 draw thanks to Matheus Cunha's deflected strike in the 89th minute.

It seemed an extreme reaction. But in a week when United lost the Manchester derby to a City side reduced to 10 men midway through the first half, then against Brighton for the first time in more than 50 years were beaten at home after giving away a two-goal lead, frustration among the fanbase is high.

Questions over fitness were first raised during pre-season when midfielder Youri Tielemans revealed United were not prioritising running.

While Cunha did not exactly agree with Neville in his post-match interview with Sky Sports, his comments will have fuelled more debate around the issue.

"At the beginning of the second half they put in more energy than us," said the Brazilian. "We cannot accept this."

Unsurprisingly, Carrick had a different take. He used the way his side tried to pressure the home team in the latter stages, leading to Cunha's equaliser, as evidence his squad is fit enough.

"The way we finished the game, actually, it didn't look like that. We finished the game really strong actually, and kept pushing. I don't think that's an issue, no," he said.

Cunha also mentioned the "noise" around United when he spoke to BBC Match of the Day.

Neville is a significant part of that noise, either directly or through his growing media empire.

Carrick has previously said he can shut it out.

It cannot be quite so easy though when United fans - who usually back their team through disappointment - followed up chants on Wednesday in disgust at the Brighton debacle by here booing Carrick's decision to take off popular England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo 11 minutes from time.

"There's always going to be certain reactions when you're making changes," said Carrick. "I've spoken to Kobbie after the game and he's absolutely fine.

"I understand at times when we are chasing the game, everyone's a little bit emotional. The supporters are, as well they should be, desperate for us to do the right thing.

"But I don't take any negatives or offence to it. I think we've just got to try and keep doing the right things to get back into the game.

"The supporters were unbelievable today, I have to say, all the way through, and stuck with the boys and supported them. At least we've given them something small at the end to take from it, and I'm sure there's more to come."

A draw at Fulham is "something small" considering the home side started the game at the foot of the Premier League - and have now swapped places with Tottenham.

Five points from five games leaves United 12th, an incredible 10 points behind pacesetters Manchester City already.

Their £70m summer signing Carlos Baleba is still to make his debut, and long-term injury victim Matthijs de Ligt was not involved at all, even though both were part of the squad that travelled south on Saturday.

Striker Benjamin Sesko also missed the game after suffering a recurrence of the shin problem against Brighton that he was troubled by for an extended period last season before submitting to a recovery programme that ruled him out for more than three months.

Carrick says "at this point" the extent of the damage is unknown.

This would all be pretty underwhelming were it not for the ticketing issues instigated by the club's touting crackdown that has annoyed so many in the fanbase.

On Wednesday, United will release their full-year financial results to 30 June, around which the full extent of their current debt will be revealed.

Then there is the general debate about the wisdom of new stadium, which is set to cost in excess of £2bn, with planning permission potentially submitted with the main Old Trafford masterplan, which is earmarked for late 2027 or early 2028.

Little wonder, after leading United back to the Champions League so unexpectedly last season, Carrick is presiding over a club whose supporters feel deflated, even if he does not recognise that.

"It's still a big season ahead," he said. "It's a long season and you're going to have spells through a season. That's part of the journey.

"I'm not playing it down, you know. We wanted more points, so I'm not saying everything's great. I understand the frustration. We wanted to be better and we wanted to do other things.

"But deflation is certainly not what we have within the club and within the group. The players didn't have that on the pitch today and that's what will carry us through the season without a doubt."

items.lbText:
Matheus Cunha's deflected last-minute equaliser spared Manchester United more misery after Lisandro Martinez's own goal had threatened to give Fulham victory at Craven Cottage.

Here's how I rated the players and you can see how you scored them below.

What do BBC Sport's player ratings mean?

Cunha rescues point for Man Utd at Fulham

Bernd Leno: On his toes to make an early save from Lisandro Martinez and scrambling when Matheus Cunha's effort looped on to a post. Denied Bryan Mbeumo with full-length save. 7

Timothy Castagne: Booked for bringing Marcus Rashford down as Manchester United broke in the second half. 6

David Affengruber: Excellent defence-splitting pass to release Josh King, but he couldn't finish. Exceptionally fortunate to escape after being outwitted by Cunha close to the goalline but stepped in to take the ball off Mbeumo as he looked to counter. 7

Calvin Bassey: Not the easiest game positionally as Manchester United played without an orthodox centre-forward. Got forward to create Fulham 's goal. 7

Antonee Robinson: Pushed into advanced areas in the inside forward position, which caused the visitors a defensive issue. 7

Sander Berge (Off, Larsson 76): Shot from the edge of the area turned away by Senne Lammens. 7

Shea Charles: Midfield partnership with Berge was key in protecting the Fulham defence when the visitors had extended spells of possession around the home area. Passing let him down on occasion. 6

Oscar Bobb (off Kevin, 70): Rolled an effort just wide of the post and probably should have done better. 6

Josh King (off Andersen, 79): Always looking to get on the ball and threaten. Took a good save from Lammens to deny him at the far post and his shot across goal was going in without the visitors' keeper kicking it away. Blotted his copybook by getting booked for diving. 8

Alex Iwobi (off Palacios, 70): Also tried to exploit the inside left channel when Fulham went forward. Low cross almost created a chance for Gonzalo Garcia and another deep one did for King. 7

Gonzalo Garcia (off Muniz, 79): Half a stride away from having a tap-in from an Iwobi cross from the left. 6

Palacios (on 70, Iwobi): Kept Fulham ticking over. 6

Subs not used: Lecomte, Manuel Angel, Sessegnon, Smith Rowe.

Senne Lammens: Key first-half saves to keep Manchester United level and came out bravely at Iwobi's feet to prevent another Fulham chance. Distribution could have been better and he didn't cover himself in glory with the Fulham goal. 6

Diogo Dalot: Tidy spin and dash into space to create a chance for Rashford but had too much work to do defensively as he lacked cover far too often. 6

Harry Maguire: Used his experience to draw a foul out of King as United tried to deal with Fulham pressure near their own goal. 7

Lisandro Martinez: Well-struck half-volley drew an excellent save out of Leno. He did eventually find the net - at the wrong end. 5

Luke Shaw (off Dorgu, 83): Returned from a three-match absence. Carrick's side are far more balanced when he is there. 7

Youri Tielemans: Wasted an excellent opportunity when he got no power behind his effort as he ran on to Rashford's short pass. 5

Kobbie Mainoo (off 79, Mount): Usual tidy game in possession without making the key passes. Never looks flustered. 7

Bryan Mbeumo: A lot of strong runs but, like many Man Utd forwards, nowhere near his best. Tough ask, but did he give Dalot enough defensive support? 6

Bruno Fernandes: Low shot against the post from Cunha cut-back but once more not at last season's levels. 6

Marcus Rashford (off 76, Zirkzee): Tried to set up Tielemans with a short pass but the Belgian couldn't finish. An attempt of his own before the break was saved by Leno and another, better opportunity flew way over the bar. 6

Matheus Cunha: Again started in the number nine role he doesn't seem suited to but created an excellent opportunity for Fernandes. Deflected shot hit the post and spun wide. Probably the visitors' most dangerous forward. 7

Subs not used: Darlow, Mazraoui, Mount, Yoro, Andrey Santos, Baleba, Lacey.

After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users.
